catalog_quote: [3.5.1, p. 30] There is no stress or accent system that would clearly distinguish affixes, clitics, and particles, so it is not easy way to recognize phonological clitics. [3.6.1.3, p. 33] Nonmonosyllabic /L/-toned nouns (and other words) are pronounced in isolation with a variable degree of phonetic initial-syllable stress. I initially mistranscribed some such words as having initial-syllable H-tone. ... For trisyllabic and longer stems, true /HL/-toned nouns are heard as H.H.(H…)L with the tone break near the right edge. By contrast, nonphonemic phonetic stress in isolation pronunciations is limited to the leftmost syllable of /L/-toned stems. [2.1.2, p. 4] Tones at syllable level are H, L, <HL>, <LH>, and occasionally <LHL>. ... Stem-level tone patterns can be lexical melodies, for example in a noun, adjective, or numeral that occurs at the end of an NP. However, these word-classes (especially nouns) are also subject to tonosyntactic overlays, such as {L} (all-low tone contour) on a noun followed by an adjective. Tones of verbs are entirely determined by the inflectional (e.g. aspect-negation) category and by pronominal subjects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penange is a Dogon tone language (syllable tones H, L, <HL>, <LH>, rare <LHL>; lexical stem melodies /H/, /L/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/ for nouns/adjectives/numerals, verbs lexically toneless with grammatically assigned tones, tonosyntactic overlays). Heath states there is no stress or accent system. The only stress remark is that all-/L/-toned polysyllabic words, in isolation/citation pronunciation, get a variable, nonphonemic phonetic prominence on the first syllable (which can be misheard as an initial H tone); no stress position is otherwise described.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned. Only a metrical note (3.1.2, p.10): in CvCvCv verb stems the medial syllable is 'metrically weak' (only short high i/u allowed there, syncope-prone); trisyllabic nouns have no systematically weak position.
new_statements.exceptions: The phonetic initial-syllable stress is described only for nonmonosyllabic lexically /L/-toned words in isolation; /HL/-toned trisyllabic+ nouns are heard H.H.(H..)L with the tone break near the right edge (a tonal, not stress, fact). Tonal minimal pairs rare (éjjé 'breast' vs èjjè 'Dogon person').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; the phonetic initial stress is explicitly an isolation (citation-form) pronunciation effect on /L/-toned words and is called nonphonemic. Description based on fieldwork with one speaker (per the 2014 draft title page).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Penange (pénà:ŋgè), the Dogon language of the single village Pinia (péná; Fulfulde piɲa), Mali = Glottolog pena1270 (West Dogon > Penangic). No dialect differentiation; data from one speaker. Glottolog lists no descriptive refs for pena1270 (only 'Heath 2012 personal communication'), but Heath's 342-page 2016 grammar exists openly at MPG PuRe (DOI 10.17617/2.2378134).

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015 [typescript dated 'last update December 2014']. Dogon lexical tones of stems. Unpublished comparative typescript, Dogon and Bangime Linguistics project (Moran, Forkel & Heath eds., dogonlanguages.info), 6 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Syllables can be H, L, <HL>, < LH>, and occasionally <LHL>. Contour tones (all except H and L) typically occur in monosyllabic words and in word-final syllables. ... In southwestern Dogon (Bunoge, Penange, Ampari, Mombo) and in Tiranige (northwestern), all verb forms have tones that are predictable from the inflectional form, so there are no lexical melodies.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1 (introductory notation paragraph) and p. 3, section 'verbs: distinguishing lexical melodies from grammatical tone overlays'
tone_statements.summary: Two tone levels (H, L) with syllable-level contours <HL>, <LH>, rare <LHL> (pan-Dogon statement); in Penange verbs carry no lexical tone melody at all - every verb form's tones are assigned by its inflectional category (grammatical tone only); lexical melodies are a property of nouns, adjectives and numerals (treated for Dogon generally). Nothing on stress or tone-bearing unit specific to Penange.

sources.note: Tone language (syllable tones H, L, <HL>, <LH>, rare <LHL>; lexical melodies incl. /L/; verbs toneless lexically, tonosyntactic overlays). Sec. 3.5.1 p.30: 'There is no stress or accent system that would clearly distinguish affixes, clitics, and particles'. Sec. 3.6.1.3 p.33: nonmonosyllabic /L/-toned words in isolation carry variable nonphonemic phonetic stress on the initial (leftmost) syllable. Sec. 3.1.2 p.10: medial syllable of CvCvCv verb stems is metrically weak (vowel raising/syncope).

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog dogo1299). Dogon NP tonosyntax arose from (a) a right-headed prosodic pattern in noun-modifier sequences, (b) loss of numeral classifiers, (c) transfer of tones from possessors to following possessums; reinterpretation in semantic terms (reference restriction). Penange-specific content not verified.
